title: TypeScript Fundamentals: Types, Unions, and Generic Collections
description: Learn how TypeScript adds static checking to JavaScript, model object shapes, narrow uncertain values, and use types that make common data transformations safer.
learningOutcomes: Explain the difference between TypeScript's static checking and JavaScript runtime behavior.
Use annotations and inference for common primitive and object values.
Explain why unknown is safer than any and narrow values before using them.
Model objects with interface and type aliases, including optional and union properties.
Use generics such as Array<T> to preserve the relationship between input and output types.
Model a typed user list and write functions that search, update, and filter it safely.

blocks.text: TypeScript checks your program before it runs

TypeScript extends JavaScript with a static type system. The type checker analyzes code during development or build time to identify many mistakes before the program executes. Type annotations and interfaces are mostly erased from the emitted JavaScript: the browser or Node runs JavaScript, not TypeScript type declarations. TypeScript cannot prove every runtime behavior safe, and external data can still violate the type you hoped to receive.

blocks.title: Types describe what code may assume
blocks.text: A type is a contract for values at a point in the program. Good types make assumptions explicit, guide editor tooling, and help refactoring. They are not runtime validation by themselves, so parse or validate data from APIs, storage, user input, and other untrusted boundaries.

A type annotation explicitly states the allowed type, such as let count: number = 0. Type inference lets TypeScript determine the type from an initializer or surrounding context, so you do not need to annotate every local variable. Add annotations where they clarify a public contract, a function boundary, or an ambiguous value; avoid duplicating obvious information without a benefit.

blocks.caption: Primitive annotations and inferred values

blocks.text: Function parameter types constrain which arguments callers may pass. The return type describes what a successful call returns; TypeScript can often infer it, but explicit return types can clarify reusable APIs. A function that intentionally returns nothing can use void as its return type. Avoid using any to silence errors: that removes many checks from the expression and any values derived from it.

any disables type checking for that value and allows most operations without proof. unknown also accepts any incoming value, but it requires you to check or narrow the value before using it as a more specific type. Prefer unknown at boundaries where a value's shape is not yet known, then validate it. A type assertion changes what the compiler assumes; it does not inspect or convert the runtime value.

steps.title: Accept an uncertain value safely
steps.explanation: unknown tells callers that the function can receive values of different types, while preventing the body from using the value arbitrarily.

steps.title: Narrow by checking the runtime type
steps.explanation: Within this branch, typeof value === 'string' narrows value to string, so string methods are available.

steps.title: Handle another supported type
steps.explanation: The number check narrows value to number, allowing toFixed. Each branch uses the value only after establishing the necessary fact.

steps.title: Make unsupported values explicit
steps.explanation: Values that are not strings or numbers reach the fallback. In real data parsing, decide whether to reject, report, or handle additional cases.

blocks.text: Model object shapes with interface and type

An interface describes an object shape and is often a good choice for domain entities such as User or Product. A type alias can name object shapes too, but can also describe unions, intersections, and other types. The two overlap for many object declarations; choose based on the required composition and conventions rather than assuming one is always superior.

steps.title: Define required properties
steps.explanation: id and name are required strings. role is a union of two exact string literals, so arbitrary strings are not allowed.

steps.title: Mark an optional property
steps.explanation: email?: string means the property can be absent. If present, its value must be a string unless other compiler options or a different declaration say otherwise.

steps.title: Check an object against the contract
steps.explanation: The object has the required fields and a valid role. It can omit email because that property is optional.

blocks.text: A union type says a value may be one of several alternatives. For example, string | number represents either a string or a number. Code may use only operations valid for all alternatives until a condition narrows the union. Narrowing can use typeof, equality comparisons, the in operator, discriminant properties, or custom type guards. It is how TypeScript turns an uncertain contract into a usable specific value.

blocks.caption: A union forces the code to account for both cases

blocks.text: A generic parameter lets code work with a family of types while preserving information about the particular type used for one call. Array<T> means an array of T values. A function such as first<T>(items: T[]): T | undefined keeps its result tied to the element type: passing User[] yields User | undefined, not an unrelated any value.

steps.title: Introduce a type parameter
steps.explanation: T stands for the element type chosen for a particular call. The function is reusable without discarding the relationship to that type.

steps.title: Represent the empty-array case
steps.explanation: An array can be empty, so items[0] may be undefined. The return type makes that possibility explicit to every caller.

steps.title: Infer T from each call
steps.explanation: The first array contains strings, so the result is string | undefined. The second contains numbers, so its result is number | undefined.

blocks.text: A useful type model makes everyday collection operations safer. If the array is User[], then filter callbacks receive User, find returns User | undefined, and a function that creates an updated user should preserve the remaining properties. Types help catch accidental property typos and invalid role values, but they do not validate arbitrary JSON at runtime.

blocks.caption: Filter and update a typed collection

blocks.title: Static types do not validate JSON at runtime
blocks.text: Typing fetch(...).json() as User[] only tells TypeScript what you want to assume; it does not prove the server sent valid User objects. Use runtime validation when data crosses a trust boundary. This project already uses Zod for validating structured lesson content and curriculum JSON.

blocks.prompt: What is the key safety difference between unknown and any?

options.text: unknown requires narrowing before type-specific operations
options.feedback: unknown accepts an uncertain value but makes the program check its type before using type-specific properties or methods.

options.text: unknown automatically converts values to strings
options.feedback: Neither unknown nor a type annotation converts a runtime value; explicit conversion or validation is needed.

options.text: any is safer because it reports every invalid operation
options.feedback: any disables many checks, so invalid operations can pass type checking.

options.text: unknown can only represent null and undefined
options.feedback: unknown can hold values of any runtime type; the restriction is on using it before narrowing.

blocks.explanation: unknown preserves safety by requiring evidence about the value's type before specific operations are allowed.

blocks.prompt: A TypeScript type assertion such as value as User validates that the runtime object has all properties declared by User.

options.feedback: A type assertion affects the compiler's assumption; it does not inspect or validate the runtime object.
Runtime validation requires checking the actual data, with code or a validation library; a type assertion alone is erased.

blocks.explanation: Compile-time type information does not automatically prove external data matches the type at runtime.

blocks.prompt: Which statements about TypeScript types are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: An optional property may be absent from the object
options.feedback: The ? modifier marks the property as optional.

options.text: A union type may describe more than one allowed alternative
options.feedback: A union such as string | number represents either alternative, and code can narrow it before using specific operations.

options.text: A generic always means the runtime function creates a new class
options.feedback: Generics describe relationships between types and do not automatically create runtime classes or objects.

options.text: TypeScript type declarations normally remain in emitted browser JavaScript
options.feedback: Type-only syntax is erased during compilation, leaving JavaScript for the runtime.

blocks.explanation: Types describe allowed values and relationships at compile time; they are not a general runtime object system.

blocks.title: Model and process a typed user list
blocks.context: Write a small TypeScript module for a user list. This task's editor saves the draft but does not compile or execute TypeScript yet, so validate it in your own TypeScript project.
instructions: Define a User type using interface or type with id, name, and role.
Use a union for role so only "learner" or "admin" is accepted.
Write getAdmins(users) that returns only administrators.
Write findUser(users, id) with a return type that allows for no match.
Write renameUser(users, id, newName) that returns a new array and preserves all unrelated properties.
Write firstUser<T>(items: T[]): T | undefined and explain why undefined is possible.
Include one deliberately invalid object or return value and confirm TypeScript reports the problem.
Explain why external JSON still needs runtime validation even after defining the User type.
requirements: The user shape has required, correctly typed properties.
The role union rejects values outside the two allowed strings.
getAdmins returns User[] and does not mutate the original collection.
findUser's type represents the missing-user case.
renameUser returns updated data without discarding unrelated fields.
The generic helper preserves its item type and handles an empty array.
The learner can distinguish compile-time checks from runtime validation.
hints: Use the declared User type in function signatures so the intended contract is visible to callers.
find may return undefined, so its return type should reflect the case where no user matches.
Use object spread when updating one property so all unrelated properties are preserved in the new object.
successCriteria: The module type-checks with strict TypeScript settings.
Invalid role strings and incorrect property types are rejected by the compiler.
Functions return new data rather than mutating the input array.
The no-match and empty-array cases are represented explicitly.
You can explain which guarantees are compile-time only and which require runtime checks.

items: TypeScript adds static checking but compiles to JavaScript for the runtime.
Inference avoids unnecessary annotations; add explicit types at important contracts and boundaries.
unknown is safer than any because it requires narrowing before specific operations.
Use interface/type to model shapes, unions for alternatives, optional fields for absence, and generics to preserve type relationships.
Types do not validate external JSON by themselves; validate data at runtime when it crosses a trust boundary.
